# typography

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D3 Frontend, Design & Motion (FE)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Depends on:** design-tokens
- **Feeds into:** frontend-core, component-library, forms

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** defining or reviewing a type system; setting headings, body, captions, or data text; choosing or loading font families; fixing flat hierarchy, arbitrary sizes, or unfinished prose detail.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is which token file or transform pipeline holds the values — that is design-tokens. Do not use this skill to set text color pairs; contrast pairs are chosen in design-tokens and only consumed here (FE-146).

## Rules

1. **FE-141 — Sizes come only from the type scale.** Every font size in a component is a type-scale token (display, heading levels, body, caption, data). An off-scale size is a defect (DET-VIS-012).
2. **FE-142 — Hierarchy is unmistakable.** On marketing and editorial pages the largest heading is at least 2.5× body size, heading levels step down clearly, and captions are distinctly smaller than body (DET-VIS-012).
3. **FE-143 — Case and weight vary by level and purpose.** Heading levels differ in size and, where the design calls for it, weight or case; one weight and one case pattern across every level fails review (DET-VIS-015).
4. **FE-144 — Micro-typography is finished work.** Prose uses real quotation marks and en/em dashes, uppercase labels are tracked out, and tables and data use tabular numerals (DET-VIS-014).
5. **FE-145 — Emphasis is solid.** Emphasis is achieved with weight, size, italic, or a solid accent color; gradient-clipped headline text is not a default device (DET-VIS-018).
6. **FE-146 — Body text meets AA contrast.** Body and caption text — including "muted" gray styles — meet WCAG AA (4.5:1, 3:1 for large text) on the surface they sit on.
7. **FE-147 — Two families, only the weights used.** A project loads at most two font families and only the weights its scale actually uses, self-hosted or delivered with subsetting and `font-display: swap` (or the stack's equivalent).
8. **FE-148 — Line length and leading are set per size.** Body columns run near 45–80 characters, and line-height is specified per type role — display text tight, body text open — never one leading for all sizes (DET-VIS-013).
9. **FE-149 — Fluid sizing comes from tokens.** Responsive type uses `clamp()` ranges defined in the type tokens (minimum, preferred, maximum), not per-component viewport arithmetic.
10. **FE-150 — Emoji are never structural.** Emoji do not appear as heading decoration, list markers, or iconography in the interface (DET-VIS-016); icons come from the component library's icon set.
11. **FE-151 — Inherited typography law.** The WCPM TYP parameter family applies as cited in docs/WCPM_MAPPING.md §2.4, and typography work is designed to pass the G-VIS gate family.

**Architecture must never leak into the UI.** Type carries the user's words, never the type system's. Font names, scale names, type-role labels, and the typographic system's vocabulary must never appear in UI copy — no font names in settings or about text, no scale labels, no type-system terminology anywhere a user can read it. The reader notices the voice, never the foundry.

## BAN list

- **BAN-FE-071 — Gradient headline text.** Banned: `background-clip: text` gradient fills on headlines as the default emphasis device. Defeats: DET-VIS-018. Instead: a solid token color with weight and size doing the emphasis (FE-145). Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-FE-072 — Off-scale font sizes.** Banned: any font size that is not a type-scale token value. Defeats: DET-VIS-012. Instead: the nearest scale step, or a new step added to the scale with a role (FE-141). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-FE-073 — Emoji as iconography.** Banned: emoji used in headings, navigation, feature lists, or buttons in place of icons. Defeats: DET-VIS-016. Instead: the library's icon set, or no icon at all. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-FE-074 — Monotone headings.** Banned: every heading level set in the same weight and the same case pattern. Defeats: DET-VIS-015. Instead: a per-level case/weight scheme recorded in the type tokens (FE-143). Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-FE-075 — Unexamined default pairing.** Banned: shipping the framework's or generator's default font pairing as the design without a recorded choice. Defeats: DET-VIS-011. Instead: choose families against the brand and content, record the choice, load per FE-147. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-FE-071 — Computed-style type audit.** Verifies: FE-141, FE-142. Check: automated — a script lists distinct font families, sizes, and weights rendered on each main page and diffs them against the type-scale tokens. Pass: every rendered value is in the scale and the largest heading is ≥ 2.5× body on marketing pages. Fail: block shipment.
- **G-FE-072 — Font payload check.** Verifies: FE-147, FE-149. Check: automated — the build report lists loaded families and weights; fail if families exceed two, a loaded weight is unused by the scale, or `clamp()` ranges in components are not token values. Pass: all three conditions clean. Fail: warn; a third family blocks.
- **G-FE-073 — Micro-typography scan.** Verifies: FE-144. Check: manual — scan headings and prose for straight quotes, hyphens used as dashes, untracked uppercase labels, and proportional numerals in data tables. Pass: no instances on main pages. Fail: warn and fix before release.
- **G-FE-074 — Text contrast verification.** Verifies: FE-146. Check: automated — run the design-tokens contrast script over every text-on-surface token pair actually used, including muted styles. Pass: all pairs ≥ 4.5:1 (3:1 large text). Fail: block shipment.

## Intelligence — decisions & gates

> **Judgment layer.** These decisions apply the judgment layer above this skill — `skills/frontend/design-intelligence/SKILL.md` and the theme library (`skills/frontend/theme-library/`). Settle the theme's art direction there first, then decide here inside it; where a decision below and a rule above disagree, the rule above wins.

### Decision rules — choosing type

| Decision | Read the situation | Decide |
|---|---|---|
| Family pairing | Expressive or editorial brand | A characterful display face for headings over a quiet text face; the display face is the brand voice, the text face disappears. |
| Family pairing | Product UI or data product | One grotesque family across a wide weight range; spend the second family only if editorial content truly needs it (FE-147). |
| Scale ratio | Long-form reading dominates | A gentler ratio (≈1.2–1.25) with more steps, so adjacent levels stay calm and scannable. |
| Scale ratio | Marketing or landing pages | A steeper ratio (≈1.333–1.5) with fewer steps; the display step does the persuading (FE-142). |
| Measure | Articles and essays vs docs and panels | 55–70 characters for essays; 45–60 for documentation and UI panels; hero lines are set deliberately, never run to the container edge (FE-148). |
| Body floor | Older or low-literacy audience | Body at 16px or above with open leading; never trade legibility for density. |
| Numerals | Prices, tables, metrics in the content | Tabular lining figures wherever data aligns; old-style figures belong to prose only (FE-144). |
| Loading strategy | Performance-sensitive audience or slow networks | One variable font or a system stack beats two static families; subset and swap (FE-147, FE-149). |
| Script coverage | Multilingual audience | Choose families with full coverage of the shipped scripts before judging aesthetics; a beautiful face missing a script is a defect, not a trade-off. |

### Self-check gate

- **G-FE-075 — Pre-ship intelligence self-check (typography).** Verifies: FE-141, FE-142, FE-143, FE-144, FE-146, FE-148 as judgment, not just compliance. Check: manual — the builder scores each item pass/fail on the shipped pages: (1) ★ squint test — blur or step back: heading levels still read as distinct bands of emphasis; (2) ★ on marketing and editorial pages the largest heading is at least 2.5× body size; (3) every rendered size is a scale step — no strays in computed styles; (4) body columns measure 45–80 characters at the widest viewport; (5) data uses tabular numerals, and quotes and dashes are finished typography; (6) muted and caption styles pass AA on the actual surfaces they sit on. Pass: both ★ items pass and at least 5 of 6 overall. Fail: fix, or log a written exception, before shipping.

### Anti-pattern table — symptom → cause → fix

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Hierarchy collapse — heading, subheading, and body sit within ~1.2× of each other and nothing leads | Scale ratio too flat; sizes picked per component by eye | Re-derive the scale with a steeper ratio; largest heading ≥ 2.5× body (FE-142). |
| Measure drift — line length swings from 40 to 110 characters across templates | Container widths set by layout habit, not by type role | Set measure per role in the type tokens and hold 45–80 characters (FE-148). |
| Scale without rhythm — sizes form a scale, yet pages feel uneven and restless | Type scale defined without a matching leading and spacing rhythm | Tie line-height and vertical margins to the same modular scale; leading per role, never one value for all sizes (FE-148). |
| Weight-only hierarchy — every level is the same face at similar size, separated only by bold | The display step was never created; large type felt risky | Add a display step and vary case and weight per level under a recorded scheme (FE-143). |
| Elegant gray captions nobody can read | Muted color chosen by eye on white, then placed on tinted surfaces | Verify every muted pair on its actual surface (FE-146, G-FE-074). |
| Font tourism — a fashionable display face fights the copy (condensed face, endless headlines; script face in UI) | Family chosen from a gallery, never tested against real content | Adopt a face only after it survives the product's longest real headline and a full body paragraph; record the choice (FE-147). |
| Prices and table columns jitter and refuse to align | Default proportional figures used in data | Tabular numerals for all data text (FE-144). |

# scroll-experiences

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D3 Frontend, Design & Motion (FE)
- **Skill version:** 1.1.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-23
- **Depends on:** motion, layout-responsive
- **Feeds into:** frontend-core

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** building or reviewing anything tied to scroll position — reveal choreography, parallax, progress indicators, pinned sections. This skill owns the scroll half of WCPM §7 and designs to pass the scroll-related G-MOT gates; the general motion system (tokens, purposes, reduced-motion variants) is owned by motion and assumed here.
- **Do NOT use when:** the animation is a state change or micro-interaction (motion), the scene is 3D (webgl-3d), or the real question is whether the content should exist (content skills). If the page reads perfectly with every scroll effect deleted, that is the correct baseline — this skill only adds on top of it.

## The positive standard — scroll is a designed system

The safety rules below keep scroll honest; they are not the design. On any page long enough to scroll, the scroll itself is choreographed as part of the theme's motion system (motion FE-091): the reader's descent reveals, scrubs, deepens, and progresses through the theme's world. A long page whose scroll does nothing — sections simply stacked, statically present — is unfinished, however safe it is. FE-101 remains the floor: everything the choreography adds is enhancement on top of content that is already fully there.

## Rules

1. **FE-101 — Content is visible if nothing runs.** Every section renders fully visible with JavaScript disabled, with the animation timeline unsupported, and before any observer fires. Reveal effects start from visible and enhance; content is never hidden by CSS alone waiting for a script to rescue it.
2. **FE-102 — Platform mechanisms only.** Scroll effects are built with CSS scroll-driven animations (`animation-timeline: scroll()` / `view()`) or IntersectionObserver. Per-frame `scroll` event handlers doing layout work are forbidden.
3. **FE-103 — No scroll-jacking.** The user's scroll position, direction, and speed are never overridden: no forced snapping through content, no hijacked wheel or touch handling, no auto-advance. The scrollbar remains the user's.
4. **FE-104 — Reduced motion turns scroll effects off.** Parallax and scroll-linked animation are disabled under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, inheriting motion's variant discipline (FE-085, WCPM CR-09); the static page underneath is complete (DET-VIS-041).
5. **FE-105 — Choreography paces a story; it never gates reading.** Scroll effects may sequence genuinely sequential content (a process, a timeline, a build-up). Any text the user needs must be reachable by ordinary scrolling at the user's pace — never locked behind a completed animation.
6. **FE-106 — Progress is never only decorative.** A scroll progress indicator is optional ornament. Position and progress through a document are communicated by structure (headings, landmarks, a table of contents where warranted), never solely by a progress bar.
7. **FE-107 — Pinned sections respect focus.** Sticky and pinned elements must not trap keyboard focus or obscure the focused element (WCAG 2.4.11 focus-not-obscured); a pinned header shrinks or yields rather than covering the focus target.
8. **FE-108 — Degradation is designed, not discovered.** Browser support for scroll-driven animations is uneven, so the unsupported-browser experience is specified in advance: content simply present, statically laid out. "Simply present" is a designed state, not a broken one (FE-101 makes it safe by construction).
9. **FE-109 — Scroll performance is measured.** A full-page scroll is profiled for long tasks and layout thrash on a mid-range device profile; scroll-linked work that produces jank is simplified or removed, not shipped and hoped for.
10. **FE-110 — Every long page has a scroll system.** Where a page scrolls beyond a couple of viewports, the build implements, in the theme's own language: scroll-triggered reveals choreographed per section (varied, never one uniform fade — motion BAN-FE-041); scroll-driven/scrubbed animation tied to descent (a thing fills, travels, deepens, or assembles as the reader descends); parallax depth where the scene has depth to give; a scroll progress indication in-theme (a filling jar, a route line, a depth gauge — a bare bar only when the theme is genuinely minimal); and pinned sections where a moment in the story earns the reader's full viewport (FE-113). Missing components need a recorded in-theme reason, as in motion FE-091.
11. **FE-111 — Scroll-driven values are smoothed, never raw.** JavaScript scroll effects read a *target* progress (a passive listener or observer may record position; that is all it may do) and the page's single rAF loop eases the displayed value toward it with lerp, so motion has weight and nothing jitters — not on trackpad steps, not at 120 Hz, not on a mid-range phone. Applying raw `scrollY` (or a raw ratio derived from it) directly to styles per event is banned (BAN-FE-056). This refines FE-102/BAN-FE-055: the forbidden thing was never the listener; it is per-frame layout work and unsmoothed application. CSS `scroll()`/`view()` timelines remain preferred where support allows, with the smoothed-JS path as the designed fallback (FE-108).
12. **FE-112 — A scroll reveal can never strand content.** Hidden start states are JS-gated (added by script, never shipped in CSS/HTML — FE-101 by construction). Every reveal also carries: a force-reveal fallback timeout that lands the content visible even if its trigger never fires; and re-trigger/re-check on re-entry, so a fast or smooth scroll that skips a section cannot leave it blank — the section is verified visible when it is actually in view, not only when its threshold crossing was observed. This is the scroll case of motion FE-096 and it is testable (G-FE-056).
13. **FE-113 — Pins serve the story, and earn their viewport.** A pinned section exists because the narrative has a moment that deserves to hold still while the world moves through it (tape transferring spool to spool, a sun crossing the sky) — not as decoration and never two pins competing in one viewport span. Pins inherit FE-107 (focus never trapped or obscured), BAN-FE-054 (never clip content at 360×640 or 1280×600), and FE-103 (the pin rides native scroll; it never captures it).
14. **FE-114 — The theme's scroll signature is present and merged.** Each theme in skills/frontend/theme-library/ specifies how scrolling itself behaves in its world — drilling down through ice strata, descending a sonar gauge, a pal walking the page's bottom edge. That signature is implemented and woven into the content it measures (the gauge *is* the article's depth; the walk *is* the page's progress), per motion FE-092's removal test: delete it and the page's meaning thins. A generic progress bar pasted over a themed page is the scroll form of BAN-FE-048.
15. **FE-115 — No dead stretches.** Ambient, scroll-aware life runs the length of the page (motion FE-091): layers drift, instruments tick, the scene breathes at every depth — quietly, under the one attention moment (motion FE-088), and all of it off under reduced motion (FE-104). A viewport where nothing in the theme's world responds to the reader's presence is a gap in the system, recorded and filled, not a rest.

**Architecture must never leak into the UI.** Scroll is a journey through content, never a tour of the page structure. Scroll progress, section names, pinned-scene labels, and any indication of how many sections or pages exist must never be presented as information about the product's structure — a progress indicator shows the reader where they are in the story, never how the site is assembled. Nothing in the scroll system names routes, sections, or the document outline to the user.

## BAN list

- **BAN-FE-051 — Reveal-from-hidden content.** Banned: sections styled `opacity: 0` (or translated off-view) in CSS, revealed only when JavaScript adds a class — so no-JS, a failed script, or an unsupported timeline leaves a blank page. Defeats: DET-VIS-040. Instead: render visible by default and let the observer add an *enhancement* (or animate from visible states only), per FE-101. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-FE-052 — Scroll-jacking.** Banned: overriding the user's scroll — snapping forcibly between sections, translating wheel input into custom animation, or auto-scrolling the reader through content. Defeats: DET-VIS-037. Instead: native scrolling, always; choreography rides on the user's scroll position, never replaces it (FE-103). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-FE-053 — Parallax with no off switch.** Banned: parallax layers or scroll-linked motion that continue under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`. Defeats: DET-VIS-041. Instead: parallax disabled under the reduce query, layers resting in a complete static composition (FE-104). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-FE-054 — The clipping pinned hero.** Banned: a pinned or `100vh` hero section whose foreground text or CTA is clipped or overlapped on short or narrow viewports while the pin holds. Defeats: DET-VIS-039. Instead: heroes sized to content with `min-height` (layout-responsive, DET-VIS-039 discipline), pins tested at 360×640 and 1280×600 before they ship. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-FE-055 — The per-frame scroll handler.** Banned: `window.addEventListener('scroll', …)` code that reads layout and writes styles on every event, producing jank on mid-range devices. Defeats: DET-VIS-040. Instead: a CSS `view()` timeline or an IntersectionObserver with a passive, rAF-throttled fallback (FE-102). Severity: WARN.

- **BAN-FE-056 — Raw scrollY application.** Banned: styles written directly from `scrollY` or an unsmoothed ratio on scroll events, so elements jump in trackpad-sized steps and jitter against each other at different rates. Defeats: DET-VIS-040. Instead: one target, one rAF loop, lerp-smoothed displayed progress that every scroll effect reads (FE-111). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-FE-057 — The observer-only reveal.** Banned: a reveal whose only path to visible is one IntersectionObserver threshold crossing — no fallback timeout, no re-entry check — so a fast scroll, a restored scroll position, or an unusual viewport leaves the section blank forever. Defeats: DET-VIS-041. Instead: FE-112 — JS-gated states, force-reveal timeout, re-check on entry. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-FE-051 — No-JS visibility pass.** Verifies: FE-101, FE-105, FE-108. Check: automated — Playwright loads every route with JavaScript disabled and asserts each section's text is present and visible in the rendered page. Pass: all content visible on all routes. Fail: block shipment.
- **G-FE-052 — Reduced-motion scroll pass.** Verifies: FE-104. Check: automated — Playwright with reduced-motion emulation scrolls the full page and asserts parallax layers are static and no scroll-linked animation is running. Pass: zero scroll-linked motion under emulation. Fail: block shipment.
- **G-FE-053 — Scroll-handler scan.** Verifies: FE-102. Check: automated — grep shipped scripts for `addEventListener('scroll'` / `onscroll`; any hit requires a recorded exception proving the handler does no per-frame layout work. Pass: zero unexcused hits. Fail: warn; block if the handler touches layout.
- **G-FE-054 — Scroll profile and pin inspection.** Verifies: FE-107, FE-109. Check: manual — DevTools Performance recording of a full-page scroll on a mid-range CPU-throttled profile, checking for long tasks tied to scroll; plus a focus walk through pinned sections at 360×640 and 1280×600 screenshots. Pass: no scroll-linked long tasks; focus never obscured; no clipped hero content. Fail: block until simplified or unpinned.

- **G-FE-055 — Scroll-system completeness and smoothness.** Verifies: FE-110, FE-111, FE-114, FE-115. Check: manual + automated — walk the page against the FE-110 component list and the theme's scroll signature; then profile a full-page scroll (fast, slow, and trackpad-stepped) on a mid-range CPU-throttled profile, confirming every scroll-driven value moves smoothly (single smoothed progress source; no per-effect disagreement) and no frame budget is broken. Pass: system complete and in-theme, signature merged, zero visible jitter. Fail: block shipment.
- **G-FE-056 — Force-reveal fallback test.** Verifies: FE-112, FE-101. Check: automated — Playwright loads each route with IntersectionObserver disabled/stubbed and with scripted instant jumps (anchor navigation, restored scroll) to mid-page positions, then asserts every section reaches full visibility within its fallback window. Pass: zero stranded sections under every failure mode. Fail: block shipment.

# data-fetching

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D3 Frontend, Design & Motion (FE)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Depends on:** frontend-state, ui-states
- **Feeds into:** frontend-core, data-visualisation, pwa-offline

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** reading or mutating server data from the client; setting up a query cache; fixing duplicate requests, stale renders, race conditions, or fetches scattered through components.
- **Do NOT use when:** the state never leaves the client — that is frontend-state. Do not use this skill to design the API itself (endpoints, payloads, status codes); that is D2/D4's architecture and backend work — this skill governs how the client consumes it.

## Rules

1. **FE-201 — All server reads go through the query layer.** Reads use the dedicated query cache (TanStack Query, or framework loaders/actions in Next.js/Nuxt-style stacks). Fetch-on-mount `useEffect` sprawl across components is forbidden.
2. **FE-202 — Query keys mirror the API.** Keys follow a stable scheme that names the resource and its parameters (`['orders', { status }]`, `['orders', id]`), so caching, deduplication, and invalidation behave predictably.
3. **FE-203 — Freshness is a decision per data type.** `staleTime` is set deliberately for each query based on how fast its data changes; accepting a global default without considering the data is not a decision.
4. **FE-204 — Stale responses cannot win.** Requests are keyed or cancellable so that fast navigation or changing parameters cannot let an older, slower response overwrite a newer view.
5. **FE-205 — Every outcome lands in the state matrix.** Each query's loading and error outcomes render through the view's ui-states matrix; errors are never swallowed silently and never leave a blank region.
6. **FE-206 — Retries come from the query layer.** Failed queries retry with the layer's backoff defaults; hand-rolled retry loops in components are forbidden.
7. **FE-207 — Mutations update exactly what they affect.** A mutation invalidates or optimistically updates precisely the affected queries. Optimistic updates always carry a rollback path that runs on failure.
8. **FE-208 — Production renders real server data only.** No fixture, canned, or hard-coded response stands in for a live endpoint in a production path; demo data is labeled as demo wherever it legitimately appears (WCPM DAT family, docs/WCPM_MAPPING.md §2.4).
9. **FE-209 — One in-flight request per key.** The same endpoint is never fetched repeatedly for one page render; shared data is requested once and served to all consumers from the cache.
10. **FE-210 — Offline behavior is designed.** Losing connectivity mid-session produces the designed error state, and reconnecting recovers through the query layer's refetch — not a manual reload (with ui-states).
11. **FE-211 — Inherited fetching law.** The WCPM §9 engineering rules apply as cited in docs/WCPM_MAPPING.md §2.2, and fetching work is designed to pass the G-ENG gate family.

**Architecture must never leak into the UI.** Fetching is invisible plumbing. Endpoint URLs, query names, cache keys, request timings, and fetch statuses must never appear in UI copy, tooltips, or error messages — a slow load says the content is on its way, a failed load says what the user can do, and neither names the API, the endpoint, or the query behind it. The user asks for content; the network is never part of the answer.

## BAN list

- **BAN-FE-101 — Canned responses as live data.** Banned: shipping fixture or hard-coded responses presented as live server data. Defeats: DET-FAKE-008. Instead: query the real endpoint through the query layer; if the endpoint does not exist yet, the feature does not ship (FE-208). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-FE-102 — Unkeyed requests racing.** Banned: issuing requests whose responses can arrive out of order and overwrite the current view. Defeats: DET-FAKE-022. Instead: key the query by its parameters so only the current key's data renders (FE-204). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-FE-103 — Swallowed errors.** Banned: empty `catch` blocks, silent fallbacks, or error paths that render nothing. Defeats: DET-VIS-032. Instead: the error outcome renders the view's designed error state with a retry (FE-205). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-FE-104 — Optimistic update with no rollback.** Banned: applying an optimistic change that stays on screen when the mutation fails. Defeats: DET-FAKE-011. Instead: snapshot the affected queries, roll back on error, and show the error state (FE-207). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-FE-105 — Fixture filtering sold as search.** Banned: filtering or sorting a local fixture client-side while presenting it as server search over the real dataset. Defeats: DET-FAKE-017. Instead: send the query to the server and render its results, with the result count from the server (FE-208). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-FE-101 — Network-count cache test.** Verifies: FE-201, FE-203, FE-209. Check: automated — Playwright navigates view A → B → A while counting requests; the shared endpoint is requested once, then served from cache with background revalidation per its `staleTime`. Pass: exactly one network request for the shared endpoint across the sequence. Fail: block shipment.
- **G-FE-102 — Race test.** Verifies: FE-204. Check: automated — a test delays the first of two parameter changes so its response arrives after the second's, then asserts the view renders the second (current) key's data. Pass: the final render matches the current parameters. Fail: block shipment.
- **G-FE-103 — Offline drill.** Verifies: FE-205, FE-210. Check: manual — go offline mid-session on the main views; confirm the designed error state appears, then reconnect and confirm recovery without a manual reload. Pass: error state and recovery both behave as designed. Fail: block shipment.
- **G-FE-104 — Rollback test.** Verifies: FE-207. Check: automated — a test forces a mutation to fail after its optimistic update and asserts the UI reverts to the pre-mutation data and shows the error state. Pass: full rollback with a visible error. Fail: block shipment.
[check condensed — full procedure in the source skill]

# forms

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D3 Frontend, Design & Motion (FE)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Depends on:** component-library, ui-states
- **Feeds into:** frontend-core, data-fetching

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** building or reviewing any form — signup, checkout, settings, search-with-filters, multi-step flows — its labels, validation, error handling, and submission behavior.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is server-side validation rules or persistence (D4 owns those; this skill owns what the user sees and how the form behaves), or the surface is a single button with no input (component-library covers it).

## Rules

1. **FE-241 — Every control has a visible, associated label.** Each input carries a `<label>` tied by `for`/`id` (or wrapping), visible at all times. Placeholder text is never the only label.
2. **FE-242 — Instructions come before the field.** Format hints, constraints, and password rules appear before or within the label and are tied to the control with `aria-describedby`, where forms-mode screen readers encounter them — never revealed only after a failed submit.
3. **FE-243 — Validation fires on blur and submit, never earlier.** No error appears before the user's first blur or first submit attempt (inherited R-11.4-2). Keystroke-by-keystroke scolding is prohibited.
4. **FE-244 — Errors are inline, named, and summarized.** Each error sits next to its field, names the field and the fix in plain text, and is wired with `aria-invalid` + `aria-describedby`. On submit, an error summary appears at the top and focus moves to it. One error per field at a time; never blame the user.
5. **FE-245 — Entered data survives errors.** A validation failure, a timeout, a reload, or back navigation never clears what the user typed (inherited R-11.4-1). The user fixes the one bad field, not the whole form.
6. **FE-246 — Use `autocomplete` for known data.** Name, email, address, payment, and one-time-code fields carry the standard `autocomplete` tokens so browsers and password managers can fill them.
7. **FE-247 — Required is marked in text.** Required fields say so in words ("required" in the label or legend), not by color or a bare asterisk alone; optional fields in a mostly-required form are marked "optional" instead.
8. **FE-248 — Submission is idempotent from the user's side.** The submit control disables on submit, retries reuse one idempotency key, and double-clicks cannot create duplicate records. Success ends in a confirmation (with ui-states), never silence.
9. **FE-249 — Multi-step flows stay short and honest.** 3–5 steps (target ≤3) with a progress indicator showing honest step counts; forms with legal, financial, or irreversible consequences include a review step before submission (inherited R-11.4-3). Multi-step forms save progress so the user can leave and resume.
10. **FE-250 — Signup stays minimal.** Signup targets ≤3 fields, hard maximum 5; any field beyond 3 needs a written justification in the project notes (inherited R-11.4-4).

**Architecture must never leak into the UI.** Forms speak the user's language, never the schema's. Field names, schema names, validation-rule names, and backend error keys must never become labels, hints, or error text — a field is labelled by what the user should enter, and an error is written as what is wrong for the user and how to fix it. The form's structure serves the user's task; the data model behind it stays invisible.

## BAN list

- **BAN-FE-121 — Placeholder as the only label.** Banned: an input whose placeholder is its sole label, disappearing the moment the user types. Defeats: DET-UX-022. Instead: a visible, associated label (FE-241); the placeholder may show an example format only. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-FE-122 — Color-only error signals.** Banned: marking an error with only a red border or red text color, with no message. Defeats: DET-UX-021 (see also DET-UX-005). Instead: inline text naming the field and the fix, wired per FE-244. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-FE-123 — Form wipes input on error.** Banned: clearing entered values when validation fails or the request errors. Defeats: DET-UX-007. Instead: preserve every value and flag only the bad field (FE-245). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-FE-124 — Double-submit creates duplicates.** Banned: a submit path where a double-click, retry, or refresh-resubmit creates a second record or charge. Defeats: DET-UX-024. Instead: disable on submit plus a server-honored idempotency key (FE-248). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-FE-125 — Submit that goes nowhere.** Banned: a form whose submit shows a success-looking state without a real request behind it. Defeats: DET-UX-003. Instead: a real endpoint, a real confirmation, and an error state when the request fails. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-FE-121 — axe-core form rules in CI.** Verifies: FE-241, FE-244, FE-247. Check: automated — run axe-core against every form page in CI and fail the build on label, `aria-invalid`, or describedby violations. Pass: 0 violations (automated) or zero findings under the manual form. Fail: block shipment.
- **G-FE-122 — Keyboard-only submit test.** Verifies: FE-243, FE-244, FE-245. Check: automated — Playwright, keyboard only: submit the empty form and assert focus lands on the error summary; correct all but one field, resubmit, and assert the remaining error names its field and every previously entered value is still present. Pass: all assertions green. Fail: block shipment.
- **G-FE-123 — Double-submit test.** Verifies: FE-248. Check: automated — Playwright double-clicks the submit control (and fires a duplicate request with the same idempotency key); assert exactly one record exists afterward. Pass: one record. Fail: block shipment.
- **G-FE-124 — Screen-reader pass on the primary form.** Verifies: FE-242, FE-244, FE-247. Check: manual — complete the primary form with a screen reader in forms mode: every label, hint, and required marker is announced, and each error is reachable and understandable without sight. **Human-required:** this gate's evidence is a human listening to a real screen reader; no automated or agent-produced substitute satisfies it, and autonomous completion is blocked until the human pass is recorded. Pass: the form is fully completable by ear, evidenced by the recorded human pass. Fail: warn, fix before release.
[check condensed — full procedure in the source skill]

# client-routing

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D3 Frontend, Design & Motion (FE)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Depends on:** frontend-core, data-fetching
- **Feeds into:** ui-states, frontend-state

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** building or changing the route structure of a single-page app or hybrid site — defining routes, navigation, guards, deep links, or the 404 view.
- **Do NOT use when:** the site is a set of plain server-rendered pages with no client router (the server framework's routing and frontend-core apply), or the question is what data a route loads (data-fetching owns fetching; this skill owns the URL and navigation contract).

## Rules

1. **FE-221 — Every meaningful view has a real URL.** If a user would bookmark it, share it, or return to it, it is a route — not a component swapped by local state.
2. **FE-222 — No state-flag navigation.** Refresh, deep link, and the back/forward buttons must all land on the correct view. A view reachable only by clicking from another view is a defect.
3. **FE-223 — Loaders fetch before render, errors stay local.** Routes load their data in route loaders (or the framework equivalent) and each route carries an error boundary, so a failed route renders its error view inside the layout instead of crashing the app shell.
4. **FE-224 — Unknown paths render the designed 404.** A catch-all route shows the product's 404 view with a path back into the product (inherited cure CD-06: design the 404 and error pages). A blank screen on a bad URL is a defect.
5. **FE-225 — Guards are UX only.** A route guard may redirect an unauthenticated user to login, but protected data is authorized by the API on every request, never by the router. Hiding a route is not protecting it.
6. **FE-226 — Crawlable links for indexable pages.** Navigation to public pages uses plain `<a href>` links to indexable canonical URLs — no JavaScript-only navigation for indexable pages (inherited R-5.2-3).
7. **FE-227 — One canonical URL per public page.** Every public page carries a canonical URL that returns 200 and does not redirect (inherited R-10.1-4; gate G-SCH-02).
8. **FE-228 — Navigation manages scroll and focus.** On navigation, scroll is restored on back/forward and reset on new views, and focus moves to the new view's heading or main region so keyboard and screen-reader users start at the top of the new content, not stranded mid-page.
9. **FE-229 — No full-page reloads inside the SPA.** In-app navigation uses the router's link component; a full document reload between app views breaks FE-222's back/forward and scroll contract.
10. **FE-230 — Route changes are announced.** The document title updates on every route change, and route transitions expose the loading state owned by ui-states — a silent, frozen screen during navigation is a missing state, not a fast load.

**Architecture must never leak into the UI.** Routes are addresses for the browser, not labels for the user. Route paths, route counts, the route tree, and navigation internals must never surface — no sitemap-style counts ('12 pages'), no route names as headings, no URL-shaped text in the interface. Navigation shows destinations in the user's words; how many routes exist and how they are organised stays behind the interface.

## BAN list

- **BAN-FE-111 — State-flag navigation.** Banned: switching views with a state variable (`const [page, setPage] = useState('home')`) instead of routes. Defeats: DET-UX-014. Instead: define a route per view and navigate with the router. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-FE-112 — Blank screen on an unknown URL.** Banned: a route table with no catch-all, so an unmatched path renders an empty shell. Defeats: DET-UX-010 (see also DET-VIS-032). Instead: a catch-all route rendering the designed 404 view (FE-224). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-FE-113 — JavaScript-only navigation for indexable pages.** Banned: `<div onClick>` or button handlers as the only way to reach a public page. Defeats: DET-UX-002. Instead: real anchor links to canonical URLs (inherited R-5.2-3). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-FE-114 — Router guard as the authorization boundary.** Banned: treating a client-side guard as protection for data the API serves without its own check. Defeats: DET-FAKE-002 (see also DET-VIS-032). Instead: the guard redirects for UX; the API authorizes every request (FE-225). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-FE-111 — Cold-load and traversal pass.** Verifies: FE-221, FE-222, FE-224. Check: automated — Playwright: cold-load a nested route directly in a fresh tab and assert the correct view renders; traverse five views using link navigation plus back/forward and assert each lands correctly; load a nonsense URL and assert the designed 404 view appears. Pass: all assertions green. Fail: block shipment.
- **G-FE-112 — Refresh sweep.** Verifies: FE-222. Check: manual — refresh the browser on every route in the route table during QA; each must return the same view with its data. Pass: every route survives refresh. Fail: block shipment.
- **G-FE-113 — Authorization boundary probe.** Verifies: FE-225. Check: automated — request each guarded route's API endpoints with no credentials and with a non-privileged session (e.g. `curl -i https://<host>/api/admin/users`); assert 401/403 and no protected payload in any response. Pass: no endpoint leaks data. Fail: block shipment.
- **G-FE-114 — Focus and scroll check.** Verifies: FE-228, FE-230. Check: manual browser verification — navigate by keyboard through three views; after each navigation, focus sits on the new view's heading/main region, the title has changed, and back returns the previous scroll position. Pass: all three behaviors observed. Fail: warn, fix before release.
